text: Everyone can hear the difference between a room and a recording of that room. What sits in between decides it.
For years that meant two bad options. An interface that adds hiss to everything, or one priced out of reach.
The MOTU M-Series ends that. Three interfaces — M2, M4, M6 — one identical engine, differing only in how much you record at once.
Every model carries the same ESS Sabre32 Ultra converter, delivering a hundred and twenty decibels of dynamic range on its main outputs.
The preamps measure minus one hundred and twenty-nine dBu of equivalent input noise. Round-trip latency is two and a half milliseconds.
And every model meters every input and output on a full-colour display.
Start with the smallest. The MOTU M2 — two in, two out.
Two combo inputs on the front, each with its own preamp gain, its own forty-eight volt phantom power, and a one-touch monitor button.
Behind it, two DC-coupled balanced outputs, mirrored RCA, five-pin MIDI in and out, and USB-C bus power.
It weighs just over a pound and runs entirely off the cable. Which means the studio goes wherever the song starts.
The MOTU M2 — twenty-six thousand nine hundred rupees, inclusive of GST.
Add two inputs and you get the MOTU M4.
The same two combo preamps, plus a physical Input Monitor Mix knob — blending live input against computer playback by hand, no routing software needed.
The back grows to match: two dedicated line inputs, four DC-coupled outputs, four mirrored RCA, and MIDI.
So two microphones stay patched to the front while a stereo synthesizer records through the rear. Four channels, and room to leave a session set up.
The MOTU M4 — thirty-two thousand nine hundred rupees, inclusive of GST.
And when two channels are not enough — the MOTU M6.
Four microphone preamps: four gain controls, four phantom switches, four monitor buttons — and two headphone outputs, in the same desktop footprint.
The four combo jacks moved to the rear, alongside two more line inputs and a fifteen volt DC socket.
An A-B switch compares your mix across two monitor pairs. The second headphone output carries its own cue mix.
Which is what six inputs actually buy you. A four-person panel. A drum kit in a single pass. A small band, live in the room.
The MOTU M6 — fifty-five thousand nine hundred rupees, inclusive of GST.
Every model ships with loopback for streaming, DC-coupled outputs for modular gear, and software to record on day one.
